title: AI Versus The Labor Market
gist: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's thesis that the US AI capex boom will lift productivity and damp inflation is not showing up in the data: since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, solid productivity growth has come alongside rising inflation, with real GDP still near its 20-year median of 2.3%. The proposed missing piece is a labor shortage that caps supply while the compute build-out adds demand.

insights.claim: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has long argued the US artificial-intelligence capital spending boom will raise labor productivity, replaying the late-1990s technology boom by supporting real GDP growth while weighing on inflation.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: This is the sitting Fed Chair's growth/inflation model, so it is the implicit reaction function behind US rate policy; if it is wrong, cuts priced on 'AI is disinflationary' are mispriced.
insights.quote: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has long argued that the massive artificial-intelligence capital spending boom in the US will improve labor productivity.
insights.locator: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has long

insights.claim: The late-1990s tech boom is being used as the template for the current AI capex cycle, implying the same combination of faster real growth and softer inflation should recur.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Watch whether the 1990s analogy holds; the analogy assumed elastic labor supply, and that assumption is the weak link to stress-test in macro forecasts.
insights.quote: Like the technology boom of the late 1990s, he expects this technological transformation to support real GDP growth and weigh on inflation.
insights.locator: Like the technology boom of the late 1990s

insights.claim: Since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, solid US productivity growth has coincided with rising inflation rather than the disinflation a productivity boom is supposed to deliver.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'AI is disinflationary' trade; argues against being long duration on the assumption that AI productivity gains will pull CPI down.
insights.quote: solid US productivity growth since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022 has coincided with rising inflation
insights.locator: So far, however, solid US productivity growth

insights.claim: US real GDP growth has continued at roughly its 20-year median of 2.3% despite the AI capital spending boom, showing no visible acceleration in trend growth so far.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark: until US real GDP prints durably above ~2.3%, claims that AI has lifted the growth trend are unsupported, and equity earnings models built on an AI growth uplift are running ahead of the data.
insights.locator: real GDP growth continuing to chug along

insights.claim: A shortage of workers, not a shortage of technology, is the constraint on the US economy's ability to expand supply fast enough to meet the extra demand created by the AI compute build-out.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: If labor supply is the binding constraint, AI capex is net inflationary in the near term; watch labor force participation, immigration flows and wage growth as the real swing factor for Fed policy.
insights.quote: AI is helping workers produce more, but a shortage of workers is constraining the economy’s ability to increase supply fast enough to meet the additional demand generated by the compute build-out.
insights.locator: AI is helping workers produce more

insights.claim: The labor market is identified as the missing variable that reconciles why better productivity has not translated into faster growth or lower inflation in the US.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Reframes AI macro analysis from a productivity question to a labor supply question, which changes which data releases actually matter for the AI trade.
insights.quote: The missing piece in the puzzle may be the labor market.
insights.locator: The missing piece in the puzzle
